nodes.title: Predictive Analytics: Social Determinants of Health & Suicide Outcomes
nodes.summary: Built count-regression models on public CDC and Census data to show how poverty, race, sex, age and disability interact in suicide deaths across 10 Southeastern states.
nodes.org: DH 5160 Analytics and AI for Health Strategies, Iowa State University

secs.b: How do socioeconomic and demographic factors (poverty, race, sex, age group, disability) interact to influence suicide deaths across 10 Southeastern U.S. states?

Merged and cleaned three public datasets (CDC WONDER mortality, CDC Disability and Health Data System, Census SAIPE poverty) by state and year in Python (pandas) and R (tidyverse). Began with OLS regression (R² = 0.679) and diagnosed severe multicollinearity; moved to Poisson, found overdispersion (deviance/df = 2.62), and fit a negative binomial model (MASS glm.nb) with a population offset and three interaction terms. Designed a Tableau dashboard (choropleth, scatter, bar) for state public-health officials. Ran in parallel with an ethnographic study (S6), whose findings added the poverty dataset.

The interaction model improved fit by about 103,000 AIC points over the main-effects model. Age × sex and race × poverty interactions were highly significant (p < .001): for White residents, each 1 SD rise in state poverty was associated with a 12.1% higher suicide death rate (IRR = 1.121). Disability × poverty was not significant (IRR = 0.9998).

nodes.title: Ethnography of Crisis Response: Barriers to Mental Healthcare in the Southeast
nodes.summary: Observed and coded an expert panel on the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline to uncover the barriers to care that statistics miss.
nodes.org: HCI 5260 Design Ethnography, Iowa State University
nodes.metrics: 9 panelists observed; 9 codes; 5 new predictor variables

secs.b: What human, cultural and logistical factors affect access to mental healthcare in the Southeastern U.S., and how can communities be supported to prevent suicide?

Contextual inquiry: passive observation of a nine-member SAMHSA expert panel (federal and state officials, first responders, peer specialists) on the 988 Lifeline. Took fieldnotes, built a codebook (including an observer-positionality code for reflexivity) and coded inductively by theme, then compared findings with the parallel quantitative model (S1).

Most frequent codes: continuum of care (17), new predictor variables (14), at-risk communities (13), systemic barriers (12). Surfaced predictors missing from the model (language isolation, LGBTQIA status, veteran status, farming-related economic instability, fear of police response) and turned them into design requirements for a public-health dashboard: co-responder mapping, continuum-of-care metrics and mobile service areas.

nodes.title: Emotive Integration Capability (EIC) for AAC Devices
nodes.summary: Co-authored a research proposal to give AAC users tone and emotion in synthesized speech, using a hybrid neural/statistical speech model and a full evaluation plan.
nodes.org: IE 5770 Human Factors, Iowa State University
nodes.metrics: 7 fundamental emotions; 14 intermediate tones; 20 advanced (14 tones + 6 nuances such as sarcasm and humor); 42-rater listener study design; 30+ user pre/post study design

secs.b: AAC devices speak in a flat, monotone voice, so millions of users cannot express emotion, tone or nuance. How can speech-generating devices add emotive prosody, and would that improve users' autonomy, social engagement and behavior?

Reviewed literature on AAC outcomes, Functional Communication Training and speech synthesis (unit selection, statistical parametric synthesis, deep neural networks), and selected a hybrid DNN–SPSS framework (Prosody-TTS) for its low data needs. Designed tiered emotion libraries (Fundamental, Intermediate, Advanced; based on Plutchik), a TOME-method use case, a hierarchical task analysis and a UI mockup. Specified data needs (about 56, 112 and 160 hours of transcribed audio per tier), a two-coder agreement protocol for labeling training audio, a listener experiment powered with G*Power (42 ratings per clip; chi-square goodness-of-fit and binomial tests), and a pre/post quasi-experiment with 30+ AAC users rated by two or more clinicians across four domains and analyzed with paired t-tests, plus caregiver and user feedback surveys.

A complete research proposal for the Emotive Integration Capability, with its constraints stated (no standard taxonomy for secondary emotions, English-only scope, no individual voice timbre) and an integration path through an open-source AAC platform.

nodes.title: How Behavior Technicians Use ABA Data Collection Apps (Interview Study)
nodes.summary: Interviewed behavior technicians and a BCBA about how data-collection apps fit into real therapy sessions.
nodes.org: HCI 5230X Qualitative Research Methods in HCI, Iowa State University

secs.b: How do behavior technicians and analysts experience and integrate data collection apps during ABA sessions, and what would make these tools better?

Literature review on data collection integrity in ABA; scoped research plan and interview guide; six semi-structured interviews (5 RBTs, 1 BCBA; Teams and in person, 30–45 min, recorded with consent); transcribed, coded inductively and organized into a codebook of categories and subcategories, with reflexivity notes on insider bias.

Most technicians use a hybrid of paper and app. Key barriers: clients reacting to devices, battery and offline failures, no undo, hard-to-find notes. Experienced technicians want visibility into progress trends and the treatment plan. Recommended free-text notes, offline mode, company devices, and BT–BCBA change logs and progress visualizations.

nodes.title: Pantry Partner: Cross-Cultural Food Security Platform (UN SDG 2)
nodes.summary: A values-driven, co-designed app that helps people in Iowa and Windhoek, Namibia find nearby food resources with dignity, and helps pantries manage inventory.
nodes.org: HCI 5300X Perspectives in HCI, Iowa State University & Namibia University of Science and Technology
nodes.metrics: 2 personas; 4 value levels with usage metrics; 21-slide pitch

secs.b: Accessing free food (pantries, community meals) is hard because information is fragmented, outdated or inaccessible, and existing tools put institutional needs ahead of the dignity and trust of the people they serve. How can a location-based tool provide food resources while prioritizing dignity and accessibility?

With an international team (Iowa State and Namibia University of Science and Technology): a values workshop mapped to UN SDGs and a team vote; user interviews plus food-insecurity and volunteer surveys; competitive analysis; personas (a new mother in Windhoek; a recently laid-off user with cerebral palsy); a values table with metrics at micro, meso and macro levels; information architecture and a prioritized roadmap; a Figma prototype; and feedback sessions, including a senior product designer.

A working Figma prototype with delivery requests for users facing disability or transport barriers, community groups, real-time notifications, and inventory scanning for pantry partners. Feedback praised donation scanning and volunteer tracking and suggested expiry alerts and earlier login. The retrospective named next steps: more iterations, full usability testing, more accessibility features, and checks on data freshness and translation accuracy.

nodes.title: Pioneers of Assistive Communication Technologies
nodes.summary: A case study of PRC-Saltillo's assistive communication devices and how user-centered design gives nonvocal people a voice.

secs.b: How have assistive communication technologies evolved, and what makes their design user-centered?

Traced PRC-Saltillo's history from a 1966 repurposed-teletype device through portable, head-pointer and touch-screen devices to the LAMP and Unity language systems; evaluated their design against four user-centered design elements (visibility, accessibility, legibility, language), drawing on company history, user testimonials and inclusive-design literature, and on my own experience teaching children to use speech-generating devices.

Concluded that PRC-Saltillo sets a standard for user-centered assistive design, and posed open questions for the next generation of AAC: expressing tone and nuance, moving beyond wants and demands, and learning vocabulary as curiosity leads.

nodes.title: NHANES Data Wrangling & Exploratory Analysis: Sedentary Time and BMI
nodes.summary: Pulled CDC NHANES 2017–18 survey data into Python, merged and cleaned it, engineered new variables, and explored how sedentary time relates to BMI.
nodes.org: DH 5160 Analytics and AI for Health Strategies, Iowa State University
nodes.metrics: 3 CDC datasets merged; 4 engineered variables; mean sedentary time 358 min/day

secs.b: How does daily sedentary time relate to body mass index among U.S. survey participants?

Downloaded three NHANES 2017–18 files from the CDC (demographics, physical activity, body measures) and loaded the SAS transport files with pandas; merged on participant ID; selected and renamed variables, checked missingness and dropped incomplete records; recoded gender; engineered age groups, a four-level sedentary-time variable (from PAD680), activity levels and CDC BMI categories with pd.cut; computed grouped means and NumPy summary statistics; and visualized distributions with Matplotlib and Seaborn box plots and histograms.

Mean sedentary time was 358 minutes a day (median 300). Box plots showed median BMI rising slightly from the low to the very-high sedentary group, suggesting a positive association between sedentary time and BMI (descriptive only, not tested statistically).
